Ava to send SOC2 + security one-pager and POC playbook link by 2026-12-05: https://redwood.com/docs/poc-playbook

header: Date: 2026-12-03 | Start: 15:02 UTC | Duration: 75 min | Attendees: Ava Thomas (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO - Nightingale), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML), Sara Gomez (Platform)
summary: Workshop to scope POC benchmark plan and decide when to use streaming vs non-streaming for Nightingale's production scoring pipeline. Agreed acceptance criteria (latency P95, throughput target), mapping of customer scripts to Redwood harness, and immediate tasks for small perf runs ahead of pilot kickoff.
topics: benchmark plan: cold start, tail, steady-state
transcript:
[00:00] Ava Thomas: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll do a quick agenda run then dive into the scripts and streaming decision. Riley and I from Redwood, Maya, Liam, Sara from Nightingale. Is that right?
[00:18] Maya Patel: Yep, that's right. Thanks Ava. We want to make sure the POC proves the end-to-end latency and cost targets before we commit to Dedicated.
[00:31] Riley Chen: Cool, so high-level, we'll run your three sample scripts through our harness. We'll compare two modes: streaming token-streaming and non-streaming (batch) request path. We'll capture P50/P95/P99, tail cold-starts, and cost-per-100k tokens.
[00:48] Liam O'Connor: Quick question, when you say streaming, do you mean gRPC streaming with partial tokens or your SDK streaming? Because our real-time scorer uses a websocket path and we have partial results expectation.
[01:03] Riley Chen: Right, so there are two flavors — the SDK streaming we provide which returns partial deltas, and then continuous streaming with lower per-token latency but more overhead per connection. We'll exercise both. We'll also simulate your websocket pattern. Might be minor naming differences — sometimes transcribe it as "kv cash" instead of KV cache in our notes, apologies.
[01:22] Sara Gomez: For us, the main constraint is the P95 < 180ms for sub-second inference on single-turn scoring at 128 tokens. Cost also matters but latency is blocking.
[01:36] Ava Thomas: Noted. So success criteria proposal: P95 under 180ms for the real-time path, P99 under 300ms for peak, steady-state throughput of ~1200 requests per minute for batch scoring, and accuracy/regression within 1% of current model outputs. Thoughts?
[01:56] Maya Patel: That aligns with our internal bar, except P99 target — can we make sure that's tail after warmup not including cold starts?
[02:07] Riley Chen: Absolutely. We'll separate cold-start measurements. The benchmark plan will include: cold-start (empty KV cache), warmup then steady-state, and extended tail (sustained load for 30 mins). We'll capture histograms.
[02:28] Liam O'Connor: On script adaptation — our current runner is python-based, some of our outputs are JSON-lines with metadata and we do context windowing client-side. Will your harness accept that or do we need adapter code?
[02:45] Riley Chen: We usually add a thin adapter. We'll take your script, add a small shim to stream tokens and manage per-request context. That's part of the action: Riley will adapt the customer runner and push a branch.
[03:00] Ava Thomas: Also, to be clear about Dedicated vs Hosted — if you need strict residency and lower jitter we can scope a Dedicated pool for the pilot, but that affects timeline and cost. We'll provide a side-by-side.
[03:15] Maya Patel: We prefer hosted for quick iteration but if jitter ruins metrics we might switch to Dedicated.
[03:23] Riley Chen: We'll include jitter and variance measurements; sometimes quantization profiles can change cost/latency so we'll include a recommended quantization config for your workload.
[03:36] Sara Gomez: On security, SOC2 and SSO are vital — can you send the security pack? We have to show compliance to procurement.
[03:44] Ava Thomas: Yes, I'll send SOC2, SAML/SSO guides, and network egress docs after the call.
[03:51] Maya Patel: Great. About the harness — does it accept long lived TCP connections to simulate websocket?
[03:58] Riley Chen: We can emulate long-lived connections. For the websocket path we'll do connection setup latencies plus streaming token latencies. For batch we'll measure time-to-first-byte and time-to-complete.
[04:12] Liam O'Connor: We also need to measure KV cache hit ratios because our feature store reuses context heavily. If cache hit is low performance drops.
[04:23] Riley Chen: We'll log KV cache hit rate as a metric and include it in the spreadsheet. Sometimes transcribers write it as KV cash or K-V cache, just FYI.
[04:33] Ava Thomas: For sample size, what's realistic? Liam, how many requests per second can you expose for the pilot?
[04:40] Liam O'Connor: We can generate up to 300 rps in a synthetic harness, but production spikes can reach 500 rps for short bursts. Our real-time path averages 20 rps steady.
[04:54] Maya Patel: The scoring payloads vary: average token length ~110, 95th at 210 tokens. We'll share histograms.
[05:05] Riley Chen: Perfect. We'll parameterize sequence length distribution in the harness. We'll also run token-level cost estimates.
[05:15] Sara Gomez: On instrumentation — can you push logs to our S3 and provide structured JSON for later analysis?
[05:22] Riley Chen: Yes, we can export telemetry to S3 and to your preferred observability endpoint. We'll anonymize request ids in the exported logs.
[05:32] Ava Thomas: Let's talk metrics for acceptance: 1) P95 < 180ms (real-time), 2) steady-state throughput target met within 10% (batch), 3) cost per 100k tokens under agreed threshold, 4) no regressions in model output quality >1% — agreed?
[05:49] Maya Patel: Agreed, pending definition of quality metric — we use exact-match and soft-F1, we'll share eval prompts.
[05:57] Riley Chen: We'll run the same eval set for regression checks. For quality we'll compute delta on your eval harness.
[06:06] Liam O'Connor: A nuance — some of our code expects streaming partials to include token positions; can your SDK do incremental token indexes?
[06:17] Riley Chen: Yes, our SDK streaming includes token offsets. We'll make sure adapter keeps that field.
[06:25] Maya Patel: On timelines, can we realistically get a pilot running within two weeks?
[06:30] Ava Thomas: Yes, if we get scripts and traffic histograms by next Monday, SE adapts scripts and runs the perf experiments, we can begin pilot week of Dec 14. That's what we suggested in the email.
[06:44] Riley Chen: We'll do two quick perf runs before pilot: a smaller streaming vs non-streaming head-to-head to help pick candidate mode. Those results will inform whether we start pilot in streaming mode or non-streaming mode.
[06:56] Sara Gomez: How will you account for warm JVM/container cold-starts? We run via transient containers.
[07:04] Riley Chen: We'll include a standard warmup window (60s) and separate cold-start tests with empty cache and fresh containers.
[07:12] Liam O'Connor: Concurrency model question: does Redwood use a single-threaded event loop per connection or multi-threaded worker pool for streaming? That affects our expected latency under high conc.
[07:24] Riley Chen: The serving runtime is GPU-optimized; for streaming we use a continuous batching loop with async IO. Under high concurrency we aim to maintain throughput with internal batching, but we will share kernel selection notes later.
[07:40] Maya Patel: Can you also include a cost sensitivity analysis? If latency gets to target only with higher-cost configs, we'll need to decide tradeoffs.
[07:48] Ava Thomas: Yes — Riley will produce a small table: configs vs P95 vs $/100k tokens.
[07:56] Riley Chen: We'll also test a quantized variant to show cost/latency improvements and any quality delta.
[08:03] Sara Gomez: Any limitations on input types? We do long context sometimes 2-3k tokens.
[08:10] Riley Chen: Our runtime supports up to 8k in most profiles, but tokenization differences can matter. We'll include that in notes.
[08:18] Liam O'Connor: For the harness outputs, can you produce a single consolidated CSV with timings per-request and the telemetry metrics?
[08:25] Riley Chen: Yes, per-request CSV plus histogram JSON and aggregated dashboard links. We'll upload to the Drive sheet and share a link.
[08:34] Maya Patel: One more — do you have an SLA for streaming tail latency?
[08:38] Ava Thomas: For Dedicated we can commit to tighter SLOs; hosted is best-effort but we'll provide observed metrics. We'll call out expected differences in the comparison doc.
[08:50] Riley Chen: Ok, quick recap of immediate next steps: customer shares scripts and histograms; Riley adapts scripts and runs 2 perf runs (streaming vs non-streaming) and uploads results; Ava shares security and pricing; schedule pilot kickoff.
[09:03] Maya Patel: Sounds good. Any risks we should be aware of?
[09:07] Riley Chen: Risk: mismatch between synthetic traffic and real production spikes; we'll try to replay shape but ask you to provide histograms & any rare long requests. Also risk: network egress constraints for on-prem setups — could affect latency.
[09:23] Liam O'Connor: We'll add rare edge-case payloads.
[09:27] Sara Gomez: We'll also check procurement checklist once we see the SOC doc.
[09:31] Ava Thomas: Great. Anything else?
[09:34] Maya Patel: No, thanks. Look forward to the benchmark results.
[09:37] Riley Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with links and the run plan.
[09:42] [Crosstalk] Ava Thomas: end of notes — send the deck.
[09:46] [End]
